Initial measurements of freshly laid eggs from a captive colony of Common grackle (Quiscalus quiscula) indicate that the initial wet weight of the zygote and its accompanying albumen and yolk is approximately 6.8 grams [Ww0 = approximately 6.8 grams]. This value reflects the minimal maternal investment per ovum at the moment of oviposition. During incubation, the embryo develops within the calcareous shell, relying entirely on endogenous yolk nutrients and the thermal environment provided by the incubating adult. At the prevailing incubation temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C], the age at hatching, defined as the interval from oviposition to the first break in the eggshell by the chick, averages 13.5 days [ab = 13.5 days]. This range of 13 to 14 days is consistent with the incubation durations reported for other temperate icterids of comparable egg size. The newly emerged nestling, a brooded chick that is altricial upon hatching, typically presents a wet weight at birth of 5.57 grams [Wwb = 5.57 grams], reflecting the residual mass of the chick after the depletion of endogenous yolk reserves during the final stages of organogenesis.

Under the thermal conditions that characterize the active metabolic and nesting period of Quiscalus quiscula, typically corresponding to an ambient temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], the nestling development proceeds rapidly. Fledging, defined as the achievement of first flight and nest departure, occurs approximately 15 days after hatching [tx = approximately 15 days after hatching] at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This relatively abbreviated nestling period is typical of many open-cup nesting passerines, where predation pressure on the brood is considerable. During this phase, the developing chick transitions from a primarily brooded state to one of increasing independence, with the downy chick rapidly emerging pin feathers. The onset of gonadal maturation, or puberty, occurs notably later in this species. Available data indicate that the age at puberty from hatching averages about 45 days [tp = about 45 days], a delay that likely reflects the substantial time required for juvenile birds to acquire the body condition and social standing necessary to compete for breeding territories in the subsequent season.

Mark-recapture studies have established that the time since birth at first brood averages 365 days [tR = 365 days], indicating that most birds do not successfully fledge their first clutch until their second calendar year. at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]This reproductive schedule is consistent with an overall life-history strategy that prioritizes rapid somatic growth and the accumulation of lipid stores during the first year of life over an immediate reproductive attempt. The capacity for reproduction is expressed through a relatively modest clutch size and a single annual nesting attempt. Data from long-term nest monitoring suggest that females typically lay between 2 and 7 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = between 2 and 7 eggs per clutch], with most clutches consisting of 4 to 5 eggs. Furthermore, the available records indicate that females typically produce only a single clutch annually [F_R_i = single clutch annually], a pattern that is common among many temperate icterids and is likely constrained by the length of the summer breeding window.

The ultimate wet weight achieved by adult female Common grackles, as determined from a large series of specimens collected during the non-breeding season, averages approximately 92.6 grams [Wwi = approximately 92.6 grams]. This value represents a more than sixteen-fold increase from the initial hatchling mass and reflects the extensive accretion of skeletal muscle, fat reserves, and plumage mass during the first year of life. In contrast, adult males of this species are notably larger and heavier, attaining an ultimate wet weight of approximately 119.6 grams [Wwi = approximately 119.6 grams]. This pronounced sexual size dimorphism, where males are roughly 29% heavier than females, is typical of polygynous or promiscuous mating systems where larger body size confers an advantage in intrasexual competition for access to nesting territories. The growth trajectory from the 5.57-gram neonate to the 119.6-gram adult male represents a more than twenty-fold increase in body mass, a striking example of the rapid development characteristic of this successful and widespread species.

Despite the considerable annual reproductive investment implied by a clutch of up to 7 eggs, the Common grackle exhibits a relatively modest maximum lifespan. Analysis of banding recovery data has shown that the maximum recorded longevity for wild individuals, measured as the total lifespan from hatching to natural death, is approximately 23.1 years [am = approximately 23.1 years] when estimated under the same thermal regime typical of their active period (41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]). This lifespan is relatively long for a passerine of its body size and likely reflects a combination of low adult mortality once territorial status is achieved and a generalist diet that buffers against seasonal food shortages. The post-reproductive period, if it exists at all in this species, appears to be brief, as most senescent adult mortality is observed shortly after the final breeding season. The combination of a delayed first reproduction and a long potential lifespan suggests a life-history strategy that balances moderate annual fecundity against relatively high adult survival, a pattern often seen in species that occupy stable, resource-rich environments.
